events.title: The financial crisis intensifies
events.description: Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy. Authorities support other financial firms as stress spreads.

events.title: Deepwater Horizon disaster
events.description: An offshore drilling explosion kills workers and leads to a major oil spill.

events.title: Japan is struck by an earthquake and tsunami
events.description: Coastal communities suffer devastating damage and begin a long recovery.

what_happened_next.text:
Apple grew to almost five times its starting value. Disney also gained, but the international basket lost more than one-fifth. The US basket ended only slightly higher, close to cash. A new device could be a major business opportunity without making every investment in the same period successful.

The financial crisis intensified in September 2008 when Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy. The Deepwater Horizon disaster and Japan’s earthquake and tsunami came later. None of those events was visible on a complete timeline when investors were reading about the new iPhone.

Apple’s gain does not mean the touchscreen demonstration made its future price obvious. The company still had to sell products, meet costs and compete. The share price could also move as investors changed their expectations. Meanwhile, the US and international baskets followed different paths through the same years. Spreading money across countries and companies changes the risks you take, but it does not make every part of a portfolio rise together.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Touchscreens and the iPhone attracted attention, while Disney changed direction and communities faced political and economic uncertainty.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The different paths mattered. A broad foreign basket and a US basket did not move alike, and one highly successful company outpaced both.
reflection.what_faded_away: A memorable product demonstration did not reveal the size of future returns. It also did not remove the risks of owning a single share.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: The financial crisis was still ahead. Even someone excited about the iPhone could not know its full business effect or the investment path.

hot_stock_outcomes.text: The iPhone became a much bigger business, and Apple added the iPad in 2010. In the quarter ended March 2012, it sold 35 million iPhones and nearly 12 million iPads. Profit almost doubled from a year earlier to $11.6 billion. These were millions of paying customers, not just excitement about a new gadget, helping support the large rise in Apple’s shares.

Office 2010 gave businesses a reason to buy updated software. In the quarter ended March 2012, Microsoft’s business-software sales rose 9%, while Windows sales also grew. Total operating profit rose 12%. Microsoft remained a profitable company through the recession, but its shares posted only a modest gain. Steady software earnings did not produce the explosive growth seen in some new mobile products.

Disney bought Marvel in 2009, and The Avengers opened in May 2012 with a record $207 million US and Canadian weekend. Its TV networks and parks were also growing. The movie business still had misses: John Carter lost money earlier in 2012. Having several sources of income helped Disney grow profits even when one expensive film disappointed, supporting the stock’s recovery.
